```{python}
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import pathviz as pv

```

# Overview

## Row {height=165px}

```{python}
pv.kpi_tiles(k)
```

## Row {height=470px}

::: {.card title="About PATH and this data" width="35%"}
**PATH** (Port Authority Trans-Hudson) is the rapid-transit line linking Newark, Harrison,
Jersey City and Hoboken with Lower and Midtown Manhattan. It has **13 stations**: 7 in
<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#2a78d6"></span>New Jersey and 6 in
<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#eb6834"></span>New York.

**The data problem.** The Port Authority publishes ridership only as
[PDF reports](https://www.panynj.gov/path/en/about/stats.html), with **no API and no CSV**.
Free machine-readable copies exist on [data.gov / NY Open Data](https://data.ny.gov/d/v5t9-im68),
which stopped in 2016, and the federal [National Transit Database](https://data.transportation.gov/d/8bui-9xvu),
which has system totals only. Neither has station or hourly detail.

**What I built.** A Python pipeline that downloads 27 PDF reports, extracts every table,
and checks the numbers against the reports' own subtotals and both government datasets.
See the *Data & definitions* tab.

**What the numbers mean.** Unless a chart says *exits*, every number is **entries**:
people passing through a faregate **into** PATH. An entry is counted at the station where
the trip **starts**.
:::

```{python}
#| title: "Ridership over time"
pv.show(pv.fig_system_trend(sysm, height=430))
```

## Row {height=540px}

```{python}
#| title: "Busiest stations"
pv.show(pv.fig_station_totals(st, height=500))
```

::: {.card title="How to read this" width="30%"}
Each bar shows how many people **enter PATH at that station** on an average weekday,
averaged over the latest 12 months.

This is where trips **start** (the origin), **not** where they end. A commuter from Journal
Square to WTC adds one entry to Journal Square in the morning and one entry to WTC on the
way home.

<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#2a78d6"></span>**Blue** = New Jersey station ·
<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#eb6834"></span>**Orange** = New York station

**World Trade Center** and **33rd Street** are the busiest New York stations, mostly from
the evening trip home. **Journal Square**, **Hoboken** and **Newark** lead in New Jersey,
mostly from the morning commute.
:::

# Monthly

## Row {height=560px}

```{python}
#| title: "Seasonality and the 2020 break"
pv.show(pv.fig_heatmap(sysm, height=520))
```

::: {.card title="Reading the heatmap" width="28%"}
Each cell is **one month's total entries** across all stations. Darker cells mean more trips.

* **Read across a row** to see a year's seasonal pattern: dips in December and summer,
  busy spring and fall months.
* **Read down a column** to compare the same month across years.
* The pale band from **April 2020** is the pandemic. Later rows show the gradual recovery.
* **Late 2012** is pale because of **Hurricane Sandy**, which flooded PATH tunnels and
  stations in October 2012.

Hover any cell for the exact number.
:::

## Row {height=640px}

```{python}
#| title: "Station explorer: pick one or more stations"
pv.picker_monthly(st, height=460)
```

::: {.card title="About this chart" width="26%"}
Tick any number of stations, or use **All stations**, **All NJ** or **All NY**. Each
line is labelled with its station name at the right end, and hovering shows every
selected station's value for that month.

What's plotted is the number of people **entering at that station**, which is where
their trip **starts**. Use **Measure** to switch between average weekday, Saturday or
Sunday, or the monthly total.

<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#2a78d6"></span>**Blue** = New Jersey ·
<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#eb6834"></span>**Orange** = New York

Sudden drops to near zero are **station closures** (e.g. Hoboken, Feb 2025), not missing
data.
:::

# Hourly

## Row {height=470px}

```{python}
#| title: "A day on PATH: before, during and after the pandemic"
pv.show(pv.fig_day_curve(h, height=430))
```

```{python}
#| title: "Is the rush hour coming back?"
pv.show(pv.fig_peak_share(h, height=430))
```

## Row {height=110px}

::: {.card}
**Left:** people entering PATH each hour, system-wide, for 2019 (dotted grey), 2021 and
the latest full year (blue). Use the menu to switch weekday, Saturday or Sunday. The
morning and evening peaks are still there but much lower. **Right:** the share of all
weekday entries that happen in the four rush hours. Lower means trips are spread more
evenly through the day. It has **not** returned to pre-2020 levels.
:::

## Row {height=560px}

```{python}
#| title: "Where trips start and end, by hour"
pv.show(pv.fig_station_hour(h, height=520))
```

::: {.card title="Entries vs. exits" width="30%"}
Use the menu to switch between:

* **Entries: trip starts here.** People going *into* PATH at this station.
* **Exits: trip ends here.** People coming *out* of PATH at this station.

Each row shows a station's day as **percentages of its daily total**, so small and large
stations can be compared. The white line separates the 7 **NJ** stations (top) from the
6 **NY** stations (bottom).

**The pattern:** every NJ station has its busiest *entry* hour in the morning, as people
leave home. Every NY station has its busiest *entry* hour around 5 pm, as people head back.
Switch to *Exits* to see the mirror image.
:::

## Row {height=700px}

```{python}
#| title: "Every month since 2017, hour by hour (weekdays, all stations, entries)"
pv.show(pv.fig_hour_month(h, height=660))
```

## Row {height=640px}

```{python}
#| title: "Hourly station explorer: pick one or more stations"
pv.picker_hourly(h, height=460)
```

::: {.card title="About this chart" width="26%"}
Pick stations, a **period** (every year since 2017, plus the July 2014 and November 2016
one-month snapshots), a **day type**, and whether to show:

* **Entries**: people *starting* their trip at the station
* **Exits**: people *ending* their trip there

At a home station (most of NJ), entries peak in the morning and exits in the evening.
At a work station (most of Manhattan), it's the reverse. For the gap between the two,
see the **Entries vs. exits** tab.
:::

# Entries vs. exits

## Row {height=150px}

::: {.card title="Do as many people leave a station as enter it?"}
For each station this compares the average weekday **entries** (trips that **start**
there) with **exits** (trips that **end** there). Riders only tap in, so exits are counted
by the **exit turnstiles and faregates**, with no fare involved. Over a whole day, a busy
station's entries and exits should be roughly equal, because most people make a round
trip. Big gaps point to something the counts aren't capturing. Use the menu on the
slope chart to switch between periods. The heatmap shows every period at once.
:::

## Row {height=660px}

```{python}
#| title: "Slope chart: entries → exits (steeper line = bigger gap; bold lines differ by 20%+)"
pv.show(pv.fig_entry_exit_slope(h, height=620))
```

## Row {height=560px}

```{python}
#| title: "Every period at once: exits vs. entries (% difference)"
pv.show(pv.fig_entry_exit_heatmap(h, height=520))
```

::: {.card title="What stands out" width="28%"}
<span class="legend-chip" style="background:#a8282a"></span>**Red** = more exits than
entries · <span class="legend-chip" style="background:#184f95"></span>**Blue** = fewer
exits than entries · * = one-month snapshot.

* **Before 2020, entries and exits matched closely.** Most stations were within ±5%, and
  the system as a whole within ±1%.
* **Since 2020, exits exceed entries at most stations.** System-wide the gap is about
  +10%, and it's largest at 23rd St, 14th St, 9th St and Newark (+26% to +39% in 2025).
* **33rd Street is the exception every year:** consistently 9–29% *fewer* exits than
  entries.
* **The reports don't explain the gaps.** Possible reasons include entries that aren't
  counted (cross-honor, freewheeled entries, fare evasion), riders leaving through exits
  that aren't counted, and the move to new TAPP faregates. Treat these as open questions,
  not conclusions.
:::
